title: Combinatorics Basics
tagline: Counting with permutations, combinations, and Pascal — plus nCr mod p at scale.

intuition.analogy: Choosing a 3-person committee from 10 people: order doesn't matter, so you count arrangements (10·9·8) then divide out the orderings of the chosen 3 (3!). That's exactly C(10,3).
paragraphs: Combinatorics is the art of counting without enumerating. The two pillars are permutations P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)! (order matters) and combinations C(n,k)=n!/(k!(n−k)!) (order doesn't).

Pascal's rule C(n,k)=C(n−1,k−1)+C(n−1,k) builds the triangle and underlies many DP recurrences (paths in a grid, subsets of a size). Recognising a problem as 'choose k of n' often collapses it instantly.

For large n under a prime modulus, precompute factorials and inverse factorials once, then C(n,k)=fact[n]·invfact[k]·invfact[n−k] mod p answers each query in O(1) — the standard competitive-programming setup.
intuition.keyIdea: Permutations count ordered choices, combinations unordered; precompute factorials + inverses for O(1) nCr mod p.

steps.title: Permutations vs combinations
steps.detail: P(n,k)=n!/(n−k)!; C(n,k)=P(n,k)/k!. Decide whether order matters.

steps.title: Pascal's triangle
steps.detail: C(n,k)=C(n−1,k−1)+C(n−1,k); useful for small n or DP transitions.

steps.title: nCr mod p
steps.detail: Precompute fact[] and invfact[] (invfact[n]=power(fact[n], p−2)); then C(n,k)=fact[n]·invfact[k]·invfact[n−k] mod p.

problems.title: Unique Paths
problems.statement: Count grid paths moving only right/down.

approach: Every path is a sequence of (m-1) downs and (n-1) rights; the count is the number of arrangements = C(m+n-2, m-1).
Compute the binomial coefficient with a running product to avoid overflow (multiply by (i) and divide as you go).

problems.title: Binomial Coefficients mod p
problems.statement: Answer many nCr mod p queries.

approach: Modulo a prime p, division becomes multiplication by a modular inverse. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials.
C(n, k) = fact[n] · invFact[k] · invFact[n-k] mod p. Inverse factorials come from Fermat's little theorem (inv(x)=x^(p-2)).

problems.title: Number of Ways to Reorder Array (same BST)
problems.statement: Count orderings giving an identical BST.
problems.hint: Multiply binomials across subtrees, mod p.

approach: The first element is the BST root; values smaller form the left subtree, larger the right. The relative orders of the two groups can be interleaved in C(L+R, L) ways.
Recursively, ways(tree) = C(L+R, L) · ways(left) · ways(right). The answer is ways(nums) - 1 (excluding the original ordering), modulo 1e9+7. Precompute Pascal's triangle for the binomials.

problems.title: Distinct Subsequences
problems.statement: Count distinct subsequences equal to a target.
problems.hint: Counting DP closely tied to combinatorial choices.

approach: dp[i][j] = number of subsequences of s[:i] equal to t[:j].
If s[i-1]==t[j-1] we either use it (dp[i-1][j-1]) or skip it (dp[i-1][j]); otherwise only skip. Base: dp[i][0]=1 (empty target).
